utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just have the headphones put on, please, Mr. Raider. Would you just have him put his headphones on, please. Good morning, Mr. Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell the Chamber briefly about your career, your schooling, and your duties in the VJ.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I completed my secondary schooling, then I went on to the military academy, and then I completed the higher military academy. I started as a platoon commander. I moved through all the other duties, and eventually I became head of communications and electronic operations of the Main Staff for communications infomatics and electronic operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. And what were your duties in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Chief of sector for communications, infomatics and electronic operations and I was also assistant Chief of Staff for that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, very often in our documents we come across the word VIED, I suppose that is the abbreviation for your sector, communication, infomatics and electronic operations.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that sector comprised?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the name speaks for itself, three administrations: Communications, informatics, and electronic actions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Visnjic's microphone please be switched off as the witness answers questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What were the tasks of the communications [Realtime transcript read in error missing word "communications"] administration department?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: In the system of command it was supposed to secure protected telecommunication and communication with units with regard to their levels. For each level there was a unit that made sure communications ran smoothly and in a protected manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The infomatics sector or department?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: They were in charge of IT for the command, but up until 1998 and 1999, that went up to the corps level and that was as far as it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And lastly electronic operations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: They were supposed to gather information through electronic surveillance and radio surveillance and submit this information to the relevant bodies for further processing and analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Electronic surveillance and radio surveillance, that is what you said, isn't it? In intelligence documents particularly we often come across the following explanation: Information was received by radio surveillance or electronic surveillance or from VIED, that's your department, and so on and so forth. Tell me, sir, your electronic operations administration or any of the lower-level units in 1998 and 1999 were they monitoring and processing information in relation to the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we weren't processing information. We received information and submitted it to the relevant bodies for further processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, how exactly did communications work, I mean the system used by the Kosovo Liberation Army in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout this period they used hand-held radio-sets. They would talk openly, not in a code. They would have up to 20 participants in a certain network. As soon as the number exceeded 20 they would switch to a different network. For the most part they didn't use any codes. As soon as they used up one location, they would switch to another. They had light equipment that was easy to transport, that was until the arrival of the verification mission. After that I assume - I cannot be certain - they had better equipment and then in their communications encryption was often used, it was scrambling for the most part, it wasn't state-to-the-art protection, but at a lower command level it was very difficult to track down. So much for their features, the features of their communication, but if I may just add something --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with with your leave, I think that we have an error in transcript, page 2, line 18, the question which Mr. Visnjic asked the witness was: What were the tasks of administration department? I think that Mr. Visnjic said: [Interpretation] What was the task of the communications department?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, what was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, communications department, as Mr. Cepic said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please move on. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you were about to add something about the communications system, the characteristic features of the system used by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that they maintained communication with NATO forces in Albania and Macedonia. We don't know what sort of equipment they used or how they got it. They probably got it from somewhere by way of a reinforcement, but that was more powerful equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: At what time exactly were the KLA in communication with NATO?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in the second half of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, now that you mention NATO, what were the communications systems used by NATO when they operated in the territory of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part they used radio communications. This is state-of-the-art equipment. There is the option of encrypting all forms of communication, usually by satellite at a tactical level they used communication channels between the air-borne pilots, their bases on the ground, fighter planes, and AWACS. We don't really know much about the modulation that their equipment performed or its technical parameters, but we monitored their communication for the most part, we knew what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: At one point in time during the war were you monitoring their communications? Were you able to intercept communication between NATO pilots?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You have meetings of the collegium and transcripts, you see that we intercepted their conversations, especially when this was about information concerning facilities to be targeted. So we were in a position to inform our units in a timely manner. At one point we disclosed our presence, they knew we were monitoring them, and then they switched to encryption.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters could not hear the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could we please go to P933 now, General.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Interpreters can now hear neither counsel nor witness because of the noise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We seem to -- hold on. We seem to have a problem. The interpreters say that they can't hear anybody because of noise. What can we do that, if anything. You need your microphone on. No one else has a microphone on. I don't know, interpreters, what else we can do. Mr. Visnjic will switch off when he's asked his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, your page is page 6, paragraph at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For e-court this is page 9 -- page 7, rather. Paragraph 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, take the witness to the right page so he can stop turning over the pages and then go on with the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, have you got the right page, page 6?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, page 6 and page 8 and page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, just page 6, please. At the top we see your contribution at the collegium meeting of the Chief of the General Staff on the 4th of March. Can you please explain the gist of your contribution at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: By that time they had used individual planes for reconnoitre and this time for the first time there was a whole squad. These planes were used to reconnoitre possible targets in Kosovo and were providing coordinates for fighter planes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: By the 4th of March [Realtime transcript read in error "April"], I understand up until the 4th of March reconnoitre had been done on a individual basis and this is the first time that a whole squad appeared over Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, when we speak of the 4th of March, 4th of March, not the 4th of April, as the transcript says.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You told us that the KLA were in touch with NATO; did that apply in 1999 well during the war.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They maintained communication with NATO commands in Macedonia and Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was going to ask you -- I was going to ask you, Mr. Visnjic, where the witness said communication with NATO. Can you give me a reference to that. I know he said communication with Albania and Macedonia. I didn't assume NATO and I don't know if he said NATO so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wasn't following the transcript. The witness said that he was in communication with NATO and Albania and Macedonia previously. He mentioned 1998, that's several pages earlier on, I think page 4 of the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought we were talking about communication between the KLA and Albania and Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 5, line 8 through 16 talks about intercepting NATO communications and then when they found out that they were monitoring them NATO switched to encryption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but that doesn't say that there's communication between NATO and the KLA. It's that particular point that we are concerned about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That was just before that. Hold on. Just one moment. Page 4, line 22 is the question: "At what time were the KLA in communication with the NATO." Line 23: "I think it was the second half of 1998."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, at the time you were listening to radio communication between plans -- planes, radio traffic, did that in a way enable you to keep track of their potential targets?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were providing target coordinates for the locations that would be targeted. We had sufficient time to inform our units, units lower down the chain of command, and tell them which facilities and locations would be targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And you told us that it lasted up until a certain point in time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Until they realised that we were monitoring them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I think that the -- that His Honour asked you when was that point in time.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard a question, but I didn't realise it was asked of me. That was sometime in mid-April, I can't remember the exact date, but it was sometime in mid-April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have Exhibit P929, page 28 in the B/C/S, page 25 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have a page 28. I have 454 and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me help you General, do you see the numbers up there, the -- the page that I'm interested in bears the number 744, that's the last number.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: It's fine. I found it now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask: Could the microphone be moved away from the papers. We can hear just the papers shuffling, the witness's microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm just waiting for the shuffling of papers to subside.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this was the collegium held on the 9th of April, 1999, and we have in front of us your presentation. I'm interested in the last passage in what you said which begins with the word "further."

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And my question in this regard is as follows: Did you have information that there was some activity in the territory of the FRY with various people spotting for NATO planes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at first we had suspicions that such activity was going on, but at that point we were convinced that it was so, in particular once we intercepted the communication between pilots in the air who blamed a spy on the roof or something that had happened. This told us that there were spotters for certain targets, but those were mostly targets in urban areas. They would put spotters, or rather, they would put locators -- they would put locators on some targets and then it was easier for the NATO planes to target those facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now I'm interested in the situation in Kosovo. According to your information, who conducted this activity, who spotted for the planes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the AWACS. I don't think that in Kosovo there were any people putting the locators except if some Siptars did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, I'm afraid I don't understand what he means by "AWACS."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what AWACS are.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a NATO aeroplane, it's a US plane, used for reconnaissance and for guiding planes to their targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what is this about locators, Mr. Visnjic? Is this something that happened in parts of Serbia other than Kosovo, since the witness says he didn't think there were locators used in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's the way I understood the witness too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could find out what part of Serbia this was happening, since it seems slightly odd.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, first of all I want to ask you to explain what a locator is. You used that term.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: These are special devices that emit at a certain frequency, and planes then receive this signal and they can then locate the target and fire at it. That would be the simplest possible explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And the Judge asked you whether you can tell us where you suspected that those locators were used or where you actually found those locators.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if His Honour heard me. I said that this mostly happened in urban areas. Belgrade is a case in point, so is Nis airports, bridges, and later on power-plants, transformer stations, transmission lines, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Andjelkovic, how are these located on their targets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in simplest terms, civilian aviation uses radio beakons to guide the planes and pilots use those radio beakons to guide their planes to fly along a certain path and this is a kind of radio beakon that is used to guide planes to their targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if this matters, Mr. Visnjic, you'll need to have it explained more clearly to me; if it doesn't matter, then just move on. I have no idea how these locators are either put on place or picked up by the flights.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I think that His Honour actually wanted to ask you -- or let me ask you. Do you know how those locators were set on the targets or where did those locators come from?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how they came to our territory, but people would set them close to the target that was supposed to be targeted. These are autonomous devices. They have certain amount of power supply, autonomous power supply, and they emit at a certain frequency. I explained. I don't know whether you understood me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand now -- I understand now. I just wanted to be clear in my mind that it was infiltrators that were suspected of putting them there. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, when you say that these were autonomous devices, could you please tell us, how long were they able to function with the power supply that they had? How long could they actually emit this signal?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were autonomous and they were able to operate for long enough to enable the pilots to actually get their signal, a couple of hours, maybe up to five hours. It depended on the amount of energy that they actually used.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, could you please explain to us what kind of communications equipment were used by the VJ in 1998 and 1999, what were the characteristics?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there's no difference between 1998 and 1999. The Yugoslav Army system was organized according to the levels of command in terms of personnel, radio relay systems, and radio system. 90 per cent -- almost 90 per cent of all the communications that were available in peacetime, mobilisation, and imminent threat of war were used as the communications system and there were some additional radio sets that were used. As the war began, as the units joined the war, radio communications were used up to the corps level. At the lower levels of command from brigade down to squad, they used only the radio system, and quite soon the radio system was jammed and the communication is impossible. From operational and strategic level we were able to encrypt our written and spoken communication, but from brigade down there was no this possibility. That would be the briefest description of the communications system in the Army of Yugoslavia. I can add --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. At the collegium meetings you spoke about the communications system several times. This was your area of expertise. Now I would like us to look at a collegium meeting, again that's one of the 4th of March, that's 5933, page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear the page reference because of the papers shuffling.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 10 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D, or rather, sorry, P5933 -- P933.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you were able to find the page, it bears the reference 871 up there at the top. I'm just waiting for the Trial Chamber to get the page up. Yes, that's fine. We can see it in English. Could you now tell me again, you're talking about the use of mobile telephones. Could you explain to the Judges in detail what this was all about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some officers used mobile phones to communicate with their immediate subordinate units, and that was very dangerous and highly destructive, because it is very easy to discover the intentions of the unit and the operations of the unit in combat operations. The problem was not only in mobile phones, but also hand-held radio sets that were used. We intervened several times to prohibit the use of mobile phones, but apparently to no avail. Officers continued to use mobile phones to tell -- to say where they were, what was happening in the unit, what the opposite side especially -- and the oppose side, especially Siptars, used that to great effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, if I understand you correctly, General, you had information because you intercepted, you monitored, radio traffic that despite this ban they continued using radio sets and mobile phones. And in this manner some data considered confidential actually were confidential no more, it is possible for them to be intercepted?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The data --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Dimitrijevic took the floor after you --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this is a translation issue, but I would like General Andjelkovic to read to us the way he sees this sentence that General Dimitrijevic said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: "Practically the entire Grom 3 was blown in this manner."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Here in the -- in the translation we have the 3rd Army and that's not what it was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's a code-name for an operation that was to be launched if NATO ever launched a ground invasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you please move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we also have the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It says here: "The attacks on the column are the consequence of open communication."

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is what you said. What is this all about, General?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously there was some conversation over mobile phones or radio hand-sets. The other side heard that and our marching column came under the attack by the enemy. That's what this is all about. This is more evidence proving that it was easy to monitor the movements of our forces through conversations over mobile phones and radio hand-sets.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, thank you. Now I would like us to look at P931, page 13, and could you please not shuffle the papers for a moment because the interpreters have a problem, they hear the shuffling. That's page 13 in e-court. And, General, that's on page 11 in the papers that you have in front of you that begins with number 832, that's page 15 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's page 15 in the English version. I don't think that we have the relevant part.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is the collegium from the 2nd of February, 1999, again we have your intervention, and I'm interested in the third paragraph in what you said in that meeting, that's on the next page, actually, in B/C/S and in English it begins on this page, it begins with the word "the next dilemma has to do -- that I have to face is the issue of the competence of the army."

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'll read the following sentence. "If it's --" --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: "If it's true that the subordinates are doing what they're not supposed to be doing and reporting to us and that they didn't do that and we have adequate information that they did that and nobody's taking any responsibility or bearing any consequences for that. I couldn't possibly agree with that. It's perfectly right for someone to raise the issue of our competence."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what was your contribution to that exactly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: The previous question about the attack on that column and the mobile phones being used which was something that wasn't called for. This was about the too liberal use of mobile phones and hand-held radio sets. We sent out warnings. We warned subordinate units to try to stop this type of equipment from being misused. However, this did not receive appropriate support at a subordinate level, and the 10th of August meeting, 10th of August, 1998, shows that. And on the 3rd of December, 1998, another meeting that shows that, and then again sometime in March and in April 1999. No one paid this any heed, especially the MUP units, and that's why I raised the issue. Were we sufficiently competent to issue an order that would put a stop to this sort of practice. That's what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. During the war what was your duty? Where were you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I was at the command post. My duty was the same as in back in 1998, head of communications and electronic operations and assistant of the Chief of the General Staff for this particular area. I was at the command post of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, were you involved in the work of the collegium? Did you attend their evening briefings throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, except for some rare meetings that I did not attend because my presence was required elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the MUP a while ago. As for the communications system that was used at the Supreme Command Staff, can you tell me this: How exactly was it set up in relation to the external factors?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a direct line of communication to the MUP units, I'm saying between the Supreme Command Staff, Chief of the General Staff, Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, and the federal MUP normally. Normally these were telephone lines. There was the option of radio communication but that would break down as soon as the cable connection was down, and then down the chain of command each level had a certain number of channels connecting them to MUP units. As for the other --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, just a minute, please. My next question, the communications system that was used in relation to lower-ranking units, how was that organized and were there any breakdowns during war operations in terms of the communication system between the Supreme Command Staff and its subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: As I said at the outset, the system was organized at all levels of command. The Supreme Command Staff had direct communication with the strategic groups, the individual armies, and commands at the operative level. You went further down the chain of command than that only if absolutely necessary, but there was nothing in place from the brigade level down. There were three different types of connections: Cable, relay, and radio. Each level of command had a certain number of channels linking them to their subordinate units down to squad level in practical terms. With these types of communication there was a certain number of channels. Cable was between 12 and 24 channels, for example; radio relay was between 8 and 12; and radio was between one and three. Depending on the level of command, the number of channels would decrease, and at the lower level of command there was normally only a single channel being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My other question about this was: Was there ever some sort of a communication breakdown between the Supreme Command Staff and the strategic groups throughout the operations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This depended on stationary knots in terms of communications. The availability of the system slowly decreased. At first the rate was 100 per cent, and then at the highest level of command, our level of command, we reached 35 per cent, that was the lowest rate. There was a period when between the strategic command and the strategic groups there were serious communication breakdowns. Fortunately this only went on for a very brief time until we could redress the damage, but at lower levels of command those breakdowns were quite frequent and quite long sometimes. I wonder how they managed to maintain any sort of communication going at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, back to the command post of the Supreme Command Staff now. Can you tell us briefly how work was organized. I especially want to know about what is normally referred to as operations duty.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: At the command post of the Supreme Command each of the administrations had their own rooms where they held meetings and went about their work. We carried out assessments, we prepared orders, we all did our jobs. In the evening hours, based on reports, we would propose measures to the Chief of the General Staff. He would transform these into specific orders. As soon as the next morning, this would be submitted to all the units. This was team-work. It was a collective effort. The Chief of the General Staff and the chief of the Supreme Command was adamant that this team-work should be pursued, and he often cautioned us that we should not be making any proposals on our own, that proposals should be a result of collective assessments carried out by the entire team, if that's what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We also heard the leader of the duty operations team; and if so, please tell us exactly what this entailed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Assistant chief of the Supreme Command, heads of sector, and individual administrations were also leaders of their respective duty operations teams at the command post of the Supreme Command. This means that each of the administrations had their own representative there who would monitor the situation on the ground over a 24-hour period. They would prepare information for the evening briefing, and in the evening they would brief the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. I was the leader of our operations team. I was in charge of our work. I collected certain information which I then submitted to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. The number varied, the number of people included in this effort. Sometimes there were 18 persons, sometimes 12, sometimes 15, depending on our needs, on what the situation required.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, are you aware of the fact or do you know of a plan being implemented by the VJ to expel the Albanian population from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I know of no such thing. I can claim with certain that not only was there no such plan, but nobody had ever thought of it to begin with. There was several collegium meetings where the Chief of the General Staff was adamant that international law of war should be complied with in the strictest possible terms, that prisoners should be treated in a humane way, and he also ordered that all subordinate units down to the last soldier must be served a hard copy of rules governing their conduct along the front line, the rights of prisoners, and so on and so forth. And this was, in fact, done and each soldier had a copy of this document on them. Therefore, I can claim with full responsibility that there was no such plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my examination-in-chief. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Andjelkovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Cepic on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just one second to prepare the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, General, good morning. My name is Djuro Cepic. I will ask you questions on behalf of General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, can you explain at the VJ level which body or which unit ensured normal functioning of the stationary communications system throughout the territory of the FRY during the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a special-purpose unit and its only job was to maintain the stationary system of communications, this was the 235th centre for stationary communication and this was a blanket body that covered all the other units that were in charge of this this, the Pristina 52nd Corps, for example, add their own centre for stationary communications. At the 235th centre was in charge of all stationary communication in the FRY throughout 1999 and even before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Can you just please slow down a little so that everything you say might be recorded.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In keeping with what you've just told us, what about all these communication units including the 52nd Corps in Kosovo and Metohija, were they all subordinated to the 235th administration?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please call-up the following document, Defence Exhibit 5D1097.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, sir, can you read the header? Do you recognise this unit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the administration of the 52nd Corps centre for stationary communication, strictly confidential, number 66-8, the date is the 29th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: No overlap, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the corps centre for stationary communication of the Pristina Corps in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So that was the administration that was subordinated to the 235th centre, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Will you please now go to item 2 of paragraph 2, communications situation and information KZ, third paragraph: Radio relay communications. Can you please read that out loud for our benefits since we don't have an English translation.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: "Radio relay communications, the 1299 line is out of order, that is the stationary communications for Djakovica, and then Mokra Gora because the Djakovica stationary communications centre is down radio relay device 800" -- fine, fine. Please tell me when I can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead, slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: "The 800 radio relay device and the Z12K are scattered all over the room -- all over the territory and the cables are disrupted. Three system blocks SCB, Butovacki Breg, numbers 2293, 2268, and 2297 from FM 200 device that were being prepared at the Pristina MUP, communications department, burned down in the MUP building that was bombed by NATO planes."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. My question: Can you explain what the targets were for NATO in terms of their long-distance strikes and air-strikes at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Their primary and principal targets, the primary and principal targets for NATO planes at the beginning of the war were communications systems, air surveillance, and reporting systems, radar systems. As far as communications systems were concerned, we had stationary nodes communication, that's SCV, regardless of whether these were in Kosovo or in Serbia and Montenegro. Therefore, at the beginning of the war immediately all the nodes were destroyed that were completely above the ground, such as Fruksa Gora but those nodes which were partly underground, they had their anti-rocket systems destroyed at the beginning of the war, but the part that was underground continued to function. Pristina, Djakovica, Urosevac, Pec, and let me not go any further into that. There were centres there that were targeted at the beginning of the war, and the stationary communications centre of Djakovica was the first to be destroyed. As the operations developed, all the other centres followed, including Pristina. Not only were these stationary communication nodes and those belonging to the army targeted, but also the PTT centres and buildings were targeted, the one in Pristina, the one in Djakovica, those were all targeted and destroyed, the intention being to destroy the command system of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, again error in transcript, page 24, line 2, I think that we missed the words "in area on Kosovo and Metohija." So could I ask again witness for this question or this clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's unnecessary. The places he's mentioned are in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I would now like you to look at PD1098.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that 5D?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, 5D1098, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, could you just please read the heading here, the unit, and the date.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: "Administration of the 52nd stationary communications centre at the corps level strictly confidential number 66-15, dated the 5th of April, 1999."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General could you read the first sentence, number one enemy, and what does it say here.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: "The Stari Trg facility was targeted, the above-ground part of the facility sustained substantial damage, the transformer station and partially the ariel pilar .

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you please tell us, General, Stari Trg, could you please tell us where is or where was this facility?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: In Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that this is close to the city of Mitrovica, Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 5D1099.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, am I right if I say that this document originated from the same administration, the 52nd?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the second paragraph in item 2 that begins with the words: "Radio relay communications ..."

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: "The following radio relay axis are disrupted" --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, no, General, we don't want to waste time. Just a quickly question. On the basis of these designations that you can see here in this document, am I right if I say that all the communications axes between the command of the Pristina Corps and the units in the wider Pristina area were disrupted?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have 5D349, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the heading.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: "The 3rd Army command, strictly confidential number 3110-18, dated the 31st of March, 1999."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It says "urgent," and then it says: "Difficulties in gathering data, report."

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the next sentence because we don't have the translation so we have to go about it in this manner.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: "Combat operations have intensified, frequent attacks from the ground and air-space, units are deployed in the area in elements, and there is a need for quick adaptation to the tactical and operational situation, particularly in the Pristina Corps area, which means that the command posts have to move quickly and it is difficult to establish reliable and protected communications. This makes it difficult and in some situations even impossible to gather in the given time and process in a reliable manner the information that has been requested."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You already said, I think that we can now conclude, that the communications systems, in particular in the Kosovo and Metohija area, was operating in difficult conditions and that it was critically threatened in some periods of the war. It was even impossible to communicate and that created difficult in communications?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, he's cross-examining and if he wants to ask questions like that which have got virtually no value whatsoever, at least for which the answers have got virtually no value for the Trial Chamber, that's up to him. Mr. Cepic, it's pretty pointless to ask that sort of question. It was more a speech than a question. We can't stop you since you're cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I can move on right now, Your Honour, if you allow. Thank you for clarification. And just one error in transcript ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, the disruptions that we mentioned and that we saw reflected in the documents, how did this affect the command in the Kosovo and Metohija area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it had a very negative impact. If you can't communicate with a unit, you cannot command that unit, so this passage that I just read out tells us that it is difficult to gather information. It was impossible to gather information, and therefore it was impossible to command the units. Because if the command posts moved quickly that means that the communications units have to move quickly, and to move a communications unit to a new location -- well, you need some time, first of all, to set up the communications system, to stabilise it, and then the command structures can continue to function. And that is why at the beginning if you listened to what I said, I said that I really wondered how at that level the command system managed to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like 5D208 to be placed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, could you please read the heading of this document.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: "The Pristina Corps command, strictly confidential number 692-1/13 ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We haven't got a link with Belgrade I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I mixed up something. Could you please read the date on this document.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: The 7th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please read what it says under paragraph 1.2, electronic operations.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: "Because of the air-strike against the Pristina post office, a part of the communications systems relied on by the VJ communications was damaged, causing the disruption of the communications with the units of -- with parts of the units of the Pristina Corps. There were disruptions with all groups except with group 21, where all communications are functioning."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Does this confirm what you just told us?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question, General: Could you confirm that the General Staff -- VJ General Staff sector that you headed sent teams to Kosovo and Metohija during the war to the Pristina Corps to control and assist them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We did send our team to Kosovo and Metohija, particularly to Pristina Corps, to assist and control, if necessary. But control was not the primary task.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Andjelkovic, we have to have a break at this stage for 20 minutes, so the court will be adjourned for that period and we will resume at 25 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, do you have cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Andjelkovic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, General. You mentioned the infomatics --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The infomatics sector or department and you said they were in charge of IT for the command. What's IT stand for, is that information technology or what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, information technology, but that's not a sector, that's not the section, it's the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I have some trouble with those terms. You also told us that you -- your group was involved in intercepting communications, but you said you didn't process that information. You received it and then you submitted it to the relevant bodies for further processing. Can you tell us, who are the relevant bodies, what organization was that that did the processing of intercepted communications?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the intelligence administration and sometimes the security administrations -- administration and if the data gathered through electronic surveillance were of interest for other administrations, then they got the data in any form, either the original form or just the excerpts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And how was the determination made as to which of those two, the intelligence administration and the security administration, how was it decided which one of those to send the materials to? Was that based on who was being intercepted or the content of what was heard?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the communications that were intercepted and their contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was it somebody in your -- I'm sorry, should I use the word "department" or "administration" or "sector," was it somebody in your group that was responsible for making that decision?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was the administration for electronic operations, and it had the section that dealt with analysis of the data that were gathered, and it gave the data to whoever needed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was the head of that administration for electronic operations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Radovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: He was to become a general later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you tell us his first name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's Dobrosav.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that the KLA were in touch with NATO, and I want to be clear, was it your information or your understanding the KLA was in contact with NATO before the conflict started in 1999? Were they in contact with NATO in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were in contact with NATO in 1998, too, because NATO was gathering information about the movements of our forces and the KLA could not monitor the movements of our forces on their own, they didn't have the proper equipment. This means that they must have gotten the information from another command and the only command that was there was NATO or some kind of a subcommand of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the way you phrased that answer, General, it sounds like you're making an assumption. You don't have any hard evidence of that, do you? Because General Naumann from NATO testified here that the -- that NATO was not in communication with KLA before the war because they deemed KLA a terrorist operation and they couldn't deal with them. He said that was part of their problem in trying to reach the October agreements because they couldn't force KLA to participate in the negotiations because NATO couldn't talk with them. I understand how you might have reached that conclusion, but that's just an assumption on your part, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can either trust what Naumann said or what I told you. I told you what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, how do you know it? It sounded that you were just forming a conclusion that they had this information, and as far as you know the only one that could have given that information was NATO or a subgroup of NATO --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you were listening closely to what I was saying, we don't need to receive information from anybody. I hope you were listening to me. I said we had no ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General, the signal seems to be breaking up. Your picture that I see on my screen is frozen and I'm not hearing the rest of your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The IT cavalry are on their way, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're asked to be patient while they try to reconnect. We have you back, General. We did not get the whole of the last answer so Mr. Hannis will ask you that question again. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd asked you how you knew because I understood your earlier answer to be that you were assuming that NATO was in contact with the KLA because the KLA could have only have gotten certain kinds of information from NATO or a subgroup of NATO. And the part of your answer we heard before we lost the signal was that you said to me: "Sir, if you were listening closely to what I was saying, we don't need to receive information from anybody. I hope you were listening to me. I said we had no ..." And then we lost you. Can you continue your answer from there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have anything to add or is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's my question. It didn't appear that you had finished answering when we lost the signal before. I wanted to give you a chance to finish if you had something else.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, it's just what I said earlier. We had a unit, or rather, units for radio monitoring, monitoring any traffic by radio communications. We tracked the KLA and we realised that they were keeping in touch with some command in Macedonia and one in Albania. Based on the language they were using, we concluded that these were NATO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What language were they using that concluded -- that caused you to conclude they were NATO forces? Were you -- they were using the Albanian language or the Macedonian language or some special NATO language?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: English and Siptar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Depending on each individual case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. I want to move to another topic. Mr. Visnjic asked you about the kinds of communication equipment used by the VJ in 1998 and 1999, and you explained that for us. You talked about however from the operational and strategic level you were able to encrypt written and spoken communication at the higher levels, but from brigade down there was not this possibility. Why were you not able to encrypt communications from the brigade level down?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the equipment plans that we had, we envisaged that the higher levels of command should be equipped first and then you went down the chain of command, but the war broke out and we simply had run out of time to provide appropriate equipment for the lower levels of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In such situations is it an alternative to use coded communications or code talk for the brigade levels and lower?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is the option of using a code book in order to keep this sort of communication confidential, but this greatly slowed down the process of command. So to the extent that this was possible we tried to have open communications regardless of the prejudice to this type of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Were coded communications used sometimes at the lower levels during the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: This was a matter of whoever was using this. Each commander decided for himself when he would use this or not use this code talk I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I seem to recall some occasions where couriers were used to transit messages; that was also done during the war, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, or liaison officers, soldiers or couriers and there were also officers in charge of signals, signals officers. This greatly slowed down the whole command system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic talked to you about -- I think it was a collegium session where you discussed the problem of the use of mobile phones by commanders, and he had you read a part where I think it was General Dimitrijevic was discussing the problems about that and said: "Practically the entire Grom 3 was blown in this manner." You told us that Grom 3 was a code-name for an operation that was to be launched if NATO ever launched a ground invasion. Were you aware of earlier plans named Grom 2 and Grom 1?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You didn't hear of either one of those?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did hear of Grom 3, but not 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how was it that you heard of Grom 3? Did you receive a copy of the plan or was it discussed in a collegium meeting? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No one received copies of Grom 3. This is a confidential document, and everybody can use it to the extent necessary. How did I know about Grom 3? If you look at the last paragraph, command and communications, who on earth do you think did that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I thought that was probably you, and to the extent there was a necessity for communications for Grom 1 and Grom 2, I thought that you might be aware of those as well.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if Grom 1 and Grom 2 were about the same issues. I am not sure if there was any necessity for a communications command. I know nothing about those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You mentioned that you were involved in the work of the VJ collegium and that you attended the -- that you attended most of the evening briefings during the war except when you were required to be elsewhere. Was there someone who attended in your place when you couldn't be there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For those collegium or those evening briefings during the war that you were unable to attend because you were required elsewhere, was there someone who represented you who attended the meetings when you couldn't?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was the head of the communication administration or some other head when I wasn't there. For the most part there was Colonel Brajovic, who was head of the communications administration, who later became a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You were discussing at page 18 today the problems caused by the NATO bombing of the communications system. You mentioned that at the lowest point you reached 35 per cent, and I want to ask you, what does 35 per cent mean in real-life terms, how that affected communications between the Supreme Command Staff and the subordinate units? What does that mean -- you were only able to communicate with them one-third of the time or with one-third of the units? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't about the time or the units, it was about the capacity. For example, you take the rate of 100. For example, we had 100 channels, links, to a certain unit at a given point in time. When certain centres had been bombed, this decreased to 35, 35 channels, which is 35 per cent in this case. And that is why availability was lower. When there were less channels, one has to prioritize as to who would be using these channels and who wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you were at 100 per cent capacity, were all channels being used all the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Depends on the amount of traffic going on. Some were available. I don't know if they were used or not. Sometimes all the available channels were being used and sometimes not a single one. This very much depended on how thick and fast the communication was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. When you were at this point of 35 per cent capacity, I think you said it only went on for very brief time. Can you tell us, are you talking about hours or days, what period of time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: This depends on the extent of damage to a certain facility or device. Sometimes this would take one or two hours, sometimes 15, sometimes 24, sometimes there was a 48-hour breakdown.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many times did you have breakdowns of 24 hours or more during the 78 days of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say exactly how many times, but at least ten times, I'm talking about the strategic command level now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reason I --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: At the tactical level it was more frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. The reason I ask, I've seen most of the minutes of the evening briefings, and you are there for most of them or if you're not, Colonel Brajovic seems to be there or some representative of your section. And most of the reports in those daily briefings seem to say that despite the damage from the bombing and despite the problems, that communications were functioning okay. Is that an incorrect assessment on my part or was there some reluctance to give General Ojdanic bad news about the communications?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me tell you this. This sort of awe never existed. Nobody was awe-stricken by General Ojdanic because was he was a reasonable man. Whenever there was a breakdown we simply never felt it was necessary to tire the collegium with that at one of our meetings. It was something we had to deal with. The collegium could do nothing to help us with this. If the work of the collegium was under threat because of these breakdowns, then certainly I would have been responsible for informing them of the general situation concerning our communications; if this wasn't necessary, I didn't say anything. I enjoyed full autonomy as far as taking decisions was concerned. Talking about the telecommunications system, I had -- General Ojdanic had transferred his powers to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where the collegium was physically located during the war? Where did you meet during those evening briefings between 24 March and early June 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: The meetings always took place at -- in a room of the operations centre at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where was the command post located?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Tejo Drajzera [phoen] Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, we had evidence about a meeting of the collegium on the 9th of April, 1999, that was held at another location, it was held at I think the VMA, and you attended that meeting, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that the only time the collegium met at a different location?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: There was that one meeting, the principal objective being to visit the wounded who were being treated at the military hospital, to raise their morale, to lend their moral support, to make them see that they were being looked after, so that's why the meeting was held there so that in addition to holding the meeting we could also visit our wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, as I recall from the minutes of that collegium session, that meeting lasted about three hours and resulted in the production of a document called a directive for I think combatting NATO. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, not a single meeting of the collegium was just simply about courtesy, a matter of courtesy. There was always something to be discussed. It would have been a waste of time for us to go to the military hospital and then just all disperse. We decided to hold a meeting there and the subject matter at that particular meeting was precisely what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you Exhibit P1481, which is the 9th of April, 1999, directive for engagement of the VJ and defence against the NATO aggression. I'm looking at what's numbered page 11. It's the next-to-the-last page in your Serbian version, I believe, General.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. I think the number is 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Command and communications, and I'm reading the English. It says: "Deployment of VSO," which I understand is Supreme Defence Council, "and the VJ GS," the army General Staff, "KM," I understand stands for command post, "in current sectors." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where was the Supreme Defence Council command post on the 9th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: The building at Drajzer Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where is -- is that the same place where the collegium met?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, who was in the Supreme Defence Council at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the presidents of the republics. When needed, the defence minister, the Chief of the General Staff were also invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Also under that title is an acronym NPKM in the Mataruska Banja sector. Can you tell me what NPKM stands for?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the rear command post, next rear command post or adjacent rear command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Because two lines up I see PKM is translated as rear command post. Can you explain the difference between those two?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No. PKM, if you look at PKM, that's rear command post; and RKM is reserve command post. NPKM, if it's necessary to leave a rear command post, the next place that they will move to is the NPKM, which is in Mataruska Banja.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So that's an alternative rear command post if for some reason the other one is not available or appropriate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I've got some confusion in connection with the Supreme Command Staff and the collegium and the General Staff. Let me explain what I'll -- then I'll ask you a question. My understanding was that the General Staff of the VJ was the body of the high-ranking generals who met during peacetime, and that once the war started this General Staff sort of transformed or became called the Supreme Command Staff. Is that correct so far?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what's the difference between the General Staff during peacetime and the collegium? Are those the same persons? What's the difference between those two bodies?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: The collegium of the Supreme Command Staff comprises the presidents and some other persons; the collegium of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, it's like the General Staff in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I think there's an evening briefing from the 29th of March, it's Exhibit 3D582, I hope you have that there, General.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I need you to go to page 4 I think in your Serbian version about two-thirds of the way down where General Ojdanic is speaking.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And my English translation says he is saying: "The collegium did not meet because I was otherwise engaged." And then going down a couple lines he says: "I will not be here all the time, being a member of the Supreme Command Staff." So that sounds to me like the Supreme Command Staff is a different body that's meeting somewhere else, is that correct, this was something different from the collegium.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Command Staff is a different body, it's not the same as the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And we've also heard sometimes the term supreme commander which everyone seems to agree referred to President Milosevic; you would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: In general terms. The Supreme Command had a number of equal members, but Milosevic was the most senior one so he was the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then along with him, who were the other members of the Supreme Command, as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: The presidents of the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. While we're on this document, can I have you go back one page to the top of page 3 in your Serbian version. And this relates to a question that Mr. Cepic asked you about Exhibit 5D1097 which talked about the communications hub in Djakovica being destroyed. Here at this evening briefing on the 29th of March you mention that it was destroyed, but if I read this correctly it says: "Of the 606 channels, 531 are usable." So does that mean you still had about, I don't know, 85-plus per cent capacity at that location?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No. When I said about Djakovica, it doesn't mean that it had 606 channels, but as for RR800 and 12K this would imply that Djakovica, the stationary node, the communication node centre there had only 12 channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And before we leave this document, just going back to the question I had earlier about General Ojdanic saying he couldn't be here with you in the collegium all the time because he was member of the Supreme Command Staff. Where were they meeting? Were they in the same building or were they across the street, do you know, how far away?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes they were in the same building that we were in, and I have no idea where they went to when and if they left the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, the question that was asked a moment ago about Djakovica and the reference to of the 606 channels, 531 are still usable, what is that referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was about the number of channels that the staff of the Supreme Command had to their subordinate commands, the total. The Djakovica stationary communication centre had a total of 12 channels from their centre, so those 12 were destroyed, not 606, with 530-something remaining in operation. Djakovica was far too small for such a large number of channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, Mr. Cepic also asked you about whether it was correct for him to say that all the communications axes between the command of the Pristina Corps and units in the wider Pristina area were disrupted and you said "yes." Can you explain disrupted for me. I take that to mean some kind of breakdown in communications, but how long are we talking about? Are we talking about a day or weeks? Are we talking about one time or 20 times? "Disruption" is a very general term. We had a disruption in our communications earlier.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had our communication breakdown, but that was just one line down and we're talking about the communications with the subordinate units. The nodes were destroyed, the nodes that were aimed at certain units, meaning that those units were left without any means of communication. I don't know how long this disruption lasted. This was not the level of command that I was in charge with -- in charge of. That was the corps command level, and they knew best what happened, how long it lasted, and what they did to remedy that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of or do you have any specific examples or where these disruptions resulted in a complete breakdown of command and control in the Pristina Corps or their subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I had received reports on some occasions that the lines of communication between the Pristina Corps and its unit were down. I don't know how long it lasted, I can't give you that information, given the time that passed, but I did have information that the lines of communication between the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps were down. And also I heard from the reports of the 52nd communications centre that there had been communication breakdowns between the Pristina Corps and its brigades. I don't know how long that lasted, but when they asked us to reinforce them with some equipment we did send it, but it takes some time for equipment to be taken out of some depots and to be sent to them. It lasted a day or two or even longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, he also asked you, Mr. Cepic also asked you about Exhibit 5D208, which is dated the 7th of April, 1999, and talked about the air-strike against the Pristina post office and damage to some of the communications systems relied on by the VJ, which caused disruption of communications with parts of the units of the Pristina Corps. How long did those disruptions related to that event last, do you know? They were temporary, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you the time because I don't know how long it lasted. I know when that happened. The cables were cut, and then you had to bridge those cables. It may have lasted some hours, a day, maybe even two days. I don't know the scale of the damage to the Pristina post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This certainly normal --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
