utterances.text: If that had been total --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you finish? I started speaking and I think maybe you weren't done.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you would agree with me that during a wartime it's not unusual, indeed it's normal and expected, to have these kinds of disruptions in your communications, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course you expected something of the sort to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you have contingencies in place to deal with those problems. They may not be at the same level of the desired communications, but you do have back-up plans and methods of maintaining those essential communications, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the air-strikes started, we made a detailed assessment about possible points that might be at greater risk during the bombing, and in those sectors we established some back-up in personnel and equipment. And if this facility would be destroyed, we were able to set-up the new equipment from this back-up depot. And the breakdown in communication lasted for as long as it took us to actually install the new equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, sir, were you aware that by the 7th of April several, perhaps as many as 500.000 Kosovo Albanians had already been expelled from Kosovo to Albania and Macedonia? You knew about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't use the term "expelled." I don't know the number of people, but at any rate I wouldn't use the term "expelled." They left themselves, in fear of the air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, some of them have testified here and told us they left because in some cases their family -- portions of their family were killed in their presence and they were directed at gunpoint by soldiers or policemen from the Serbian security forces to go to Albania, or in some cases, for example, in Pristina, they were put on the train and directed to go to Macedonia. You know about that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that some people were killed in Kosovo, not only Siptars. Why don't you say how many Serbs from Kosovo and Metohija were killed or interred. I can't claim that nobody pointed a gun at anyone, there were such cases, but that was not widespread phenomenon. Those were just isolated cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Hundreds of thousands of isolated cases?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: That's your information. My information does not say that there were hundreds of thousands. It all depends on your point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. General, were you aware of a body that we, the Prosecution in this case, say existed in 1998 and in 1999 called the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard this Joint Command being talked about, but I can claim with full responsibility that such a command, such an organ is something that is completely foreign to me. I don't know anything about that. I don't know who the members of the command were, who was the supreme chief, who provided communications for this command, who were its superiors, who were its subordinates. I would have to know all this and yet I don't know any of these elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's have a look at Exhibit P1487. This is a one-page document, General, dated the -- dated the 17th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see that's from the Supreme Command Staff, staff operations department, to the 3rd Army command, to the commander personally, which would have been General Pavkovic at the time. And its suggestions from General Ojdanic. Do you see the line that says: "Link Kosovo and Metohija Joint Command order strictly confidential number 455-148 of 15 April 1999"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you ever seen that document before today?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you see -- you saw that reference to a specific order of the Joint Command, and below that you see suggestions from General Ojdanic, who as I understand it was the highest-ranking uniformed officer in the military in Yugoslavia at the time. Do you have an explanation for why he would be making suggestions in relation to an order issued by some other body called the Joint Command. Isn't he the highest-ranking officer, shouldn't he be telling them what to do, not making suggestions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: That means that this body, this body was not superior to General Ojdanic, and General Ojdanic was not its subordinate. That's what this document tells us. That is why he is suggesting and not ordering, and he didn't have the -- any right to order, but just to suggest. That body could not have been in command of the Army of Yugoslavia or of the forces in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, this document appears to be a reference to an order that requires the 3rd Army commander, General Pavkovic, to do something, and General Ojdanic in this document seems to me to be deferring to the Joint Command by making suggestions rather than over -- taking over from them. So what was General Pavkovic supposed to do in this situation, follow the Joint Command order or follow the suggestions of his superior, General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, he must obey the suggestions made by his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question is: In this context, who's his superior, General Ojdanic or the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: General Ojdanic is the superior of the 3rd Army command because the supreme commander conferred the powers he had on General Ojdanic to command the 3rd Army, and this Joint Command had no superior authority over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, sir, I suggest that you don't know that because you told us you didn't know anything about the Joint Command. Do you allow for the possibility that Mr. Milosevic, the supreme commander, may have created this body called the Joint Command and conveyed power upon it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Andjelkovic, the interpreters did not hear your answer; could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Mr. Prosecutor said, can I allow for the possibility that President Milosevic could have formed such a body and conferred some powers on that body, I said that, yes, it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I want to ask you now about a collegium meeting on the 4th of March, 1999, this is Exhibit P933. And I want to go to the last page of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have that, General?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, it's in English. Let me find the last page -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you find the paragraph where you're speaking?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right above that I want to read from the preceding speaker, who if you go back a couple pages it appears it was General Marjanovic, who I understand was the deputy, and he appears to have been conducting this particular meeting. And he's saying: "I would ask Ljubo who took on the obligation as the fourth task to write an order to disband the command of the special unit corps." Is he referring to you there when he uses the name Ljubo? Pardon my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. That's not me. I didn't have any authority to write such things or to issue any orders to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But you're the next speaker and you talk about requests from the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army for personnel. Do you know -- what do you know about this --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am, I am the next speaker, but there are other people called Ljubo, not just myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what -- who that would have referred to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I can comment on the last passage, but I am not the person identified here, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know who that would have been, to write that order to disband the command of the special unit corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the last passage where I'm speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, right when general --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the orders came from the operations and staff affairs sector and the operations administration was the one and if I'm not mistaken this is a reference to General Obradovic, not to myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall what the decision was and why the command of the special unit corps was being disbanded?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have a comment to make about what you said at this meeting about the request for personnel, the disparate number between the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army request?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, during the air-strikes, training centres were set up to train troops, and every unit on the basis of the recruitment sent some of its soldiers to those centres. And those soldiers came back to the units, the units that had sent them to the training centres. The 3rd Army first requested the number of soldiers that it had and then an increased number of soldiers, which meant that other units that sent their soldiers to be trained in those centres should be taken out and sent to the 3rd Army to reinforce it. That is what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The last topic I want to ask you about was at the very end of your questioning by Mr. Visnjic. He asked you if you knew of a plan being implemented by the VJ to expel the Albanian population from Kosovo. And you said: "No, I know of no such thing. I can claim with certain that not only was there no such plan, but nobody had ever thought of it to begin with." My question -- my questions begin with this one: If nobody had ever thought of it, why was there a need to issue so many orders about obeying international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how many orders were actually issues, but all soldiers were warned at the beginning of the combat operations. That's for sure. That's quite obvious, but you cannot rule out the possibility that some individuals might conduct themselves in an inappropriate manner because we're talking about a large number of people in a large area. And there was no such plan, that's what I maintain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you aware of what Slobodan Milosevic is reported to have said to General Naumann and General Clark in October of 1998 when their agreement was signed about how he proposed to deal with the Kosovo problem in the spring of 1999, that is, by taking out the Albanians and shooting them, as had been done in Drenica in 1945 and 1946, did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Visnjic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this part of the question that was put to the witness is incorrect, and I think Mr. Hannis knows quite well which portion I'm referring to that's inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the spring of 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as I recall he said that he would have a solution in the spring. I may be wrong about that, but I seem to recall there was evidence about that, either in General Naumann's statement and/or in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say that's wrong, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can recall, the spring of 1999 was not mentioned. I have no objection to the rest of the question, but as far as I can recall the spring of 1999 was not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may be wrong there because I think he said in October "in the spring." He may not have said in the spring of 1999, but I believe he said in the spring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My inclination from memory is that you're correct, Mr. Hannis, however you can rephrase this to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, did you ever hear about that allegation that Mr. Milosevic had told Clark and Naumann of his proposed solution for the Kosovo problem in the terms that I described above, without a reference to 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And then if you allow for the possibility that that, indeed, was said, how can you say that no one -- nobody ever thought of it, nobody ever thought of expelling the Kosovo Albanians or killing the Kosovo Albanians to get rid of them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before -- don't answer that question. Before Mr. Visnjic gets to his feet, that's a hypothesis too far I think, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, General: I concede that you're an expert in communications, but you're not a mind-reader, you don't know what was in the mind of every individual in the high government authorities, the VJ, and the MUP, do you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when I said that no such plan existed and that it would never occur to anyone to think of such a thing, I was talking about the soldiers and the collegium where I was present. I'm talking about the military leadership, the top echelons. Now, as to what other people, civilians, were thinking, no, you're right, I cannot know what everybody was thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, you couldn't have known what was in the mind of every member of the VJ in 1998 and 1999, could you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the VJ does not have 18 people, it had several thousand -- thousands of people. I was talking about the collegium. I was in a position to know what everybody in the collegium was thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just if you allow me one correction in transcript, page 54, line 5, I think the witness also said [Interpretation] "People outside of the army were thinking." I think that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission I would like to pursue this speculation a little bit further contained in Mr. Hannis's question, whether Milosevic may have set up a Joint Command and conferred some powers on it. I would like you to look at the question the way it is phrased and the witness did not rule that out. If we were to stop there, we could have something that would be akin to manipulation. I would like to go further into this because this is a document from 1999, we're talking about the Joint Command in 1998, 1999, and so on and so forth, with such a speculative statement, with such a sentence that the witness was led into uttering. I don't think that it would take us too far. I would like, with your permission, to question the witness a bit further on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which line are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's page 48 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the line because of background noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the response is at page 49, line 7. It's just hanging there like a leaf that just fell off the branch. It's not connected to anything. That's line 20 on page 48, that's the question, and the answer is 49, line 7. So this is a typical answer ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, have you any difficulty with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Fila. Further cross-examination by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. My name is Toma Fila. I'm defending Nikola Sainovic in this case, and unfortunately I will have to take some of your time.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In answer to a question by Mr. Hannis you answered that you allowed for the possibility that Slobodan Milosevic may have set up a Joint Command of some sort and conferred something on it, some powers. First let me ask you: Do you have any idea that any such thing existed or was established or is this just pure speculation on your part?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea that something of the sort had been established, but I could not rule out the possibility that I didn't know about something that had been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the basis of your participation in the work of the army in 1998 and 1999, including the wartime period, did you notice that the chain of command was compromised anywhere in the sphere of communications where you worked or anywhere else by the existence of some kind of a Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the VJ was correspond, I never noticed any such thing. There were no disruptions in the VJ communications system by anyone, except if we talk about the army proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But we cannot get too hypothetical about this, can we?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you have noticed if there was some Joint Command during the war or even in 1998 that was a body that was superior to General Ojdanic and, by the same token, to you? Would you have noted anything like that? Could it have slipped your attention?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it couldn't possibly have slipped my attention and it never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you perhaps notice that any civilian, quite apart from Slobodan Milosevic in a manner of speaking, who was the supreme commander, the commander of the VJ in both peace and wartime, that any civilian gave any sort of orders to General Ojdanic? Did you notice anything like that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never, with the exception of President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about any subordinate officers giving orders to the commander of an entire army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've had your answer. There's a limit to how much argumentation you can present in the context where we are obliging you by allowing you to do this. It sounds to me as though you're abusing the privilege now that you've been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have the same impression, that's while I'll now desist from any further questioning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Visnjic, we have to break now, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, two questions and I'm finished with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the Prosecutor asked you about the fact that you told us about that NATO were in touch with the KLA in 1998. You were asked about the language that was used, you said English and Albanian. My question is this: What sort of information was exchanged?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, information concerning where our units were and where they were moving to, as well as information on facilities where the KLA were, or rather, the terror groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And lastly, General, who in your opinion could have been privy to that type of information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "who." You mean who was in a position to obtain such information or who was in possession of such information once this type of information had been obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What I meant was: Who would have been in a position to have this sort of information available to them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: The intelligence administration, we would gather this information, we would give it to them, and it was then available to them to do with it as they saw fit. The KLA distributed information to their own groups on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question. Mr. Hannis narrowed down the number of people for you, the people you talked about in terms of being certain that they had no plan to expel Albanians in mind. Do you include General Ojdanic in that group?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Andjelkovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to give evidence to the Tribunal. You're now free to leave once we have risen and the link is disconnected. We'll adjourn now and resume at 1.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We apologise to you all for the disruption of the schedule, but it was caused by the meeting we attended lasting longer than had been anticipated. So we'll now try to do our best to compensate you in whatever way we can. So, Mr. Visnjic, if you want another hour added on to the day, then you just need to say the word. Your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is Nedjo Danilovic, but may I just address the Court briefly before the witness starts; therefore, if the witness could be asked to leave the courtroom briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, please put -- you have a problem that you need to raise in his absence, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Danilovic, we thought we could get started quickly, but there is a matter of law to be dealt with. I wonder if you could please leave the courtroom briefly. Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first and foremost, given that there are certain indications that the Prosecutor might object and also what you said about Novkovic and this is to do with this witness, we looked at the summary again and about the summary we decided to cut his evidence short, substantially so, in fact. It will be in reference to the following issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, you can always do that, cut witnesses' evidence as you see fit, and you don't need to set that out for us. If anyone needs to know, it's Mr. Hannis, but I don't think we need to spend time on that just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While the witness remains outside, there's just another matter that I wish to raise, it's not about this witness but I would like to take this opportunity. Mr. Hannis proposed that our expert appear at the end of the trial, along with all the other experts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm going to raise that with you at the end of today's business.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just while you're on witnesses, though, I think you added a witness this week, is the name Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was difficult at first sight to see what the issue is in his evidence. If you were to ask Mr. Hannis whether he accepted that NATO may have changed their position on the use of certain weapons, then you might get an answer, I don't know for sure, but you might get an answer that makes some of this evidence redundant. And if you ask him whether these weapons included cluster bombs and depleted uranium, you might also get an answer that might cut down, on the other hand, you might not. I'm not saying for sure. We're not here, as you know, to deal with the rights and wrongs of NATO conduct. We are only here to deal with NATO conduct so far as it may be relevant to the issues in this trial, such as the movement of population. So give some thought to whether the evidence heralded from him is all entirely necessary. Now we can have Mr. Danilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. Danilovic, we dealt with the issue that arose. Could you now make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe your military career briefly for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and briefly your duties in 1999.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: By all means. After completing my secondary education I graduated from the JNA military academy in 1979. I was the third-best rated student that year. In 1980 I was the best-placed student at the security school. In 1992 I completed the General Staff academy of the JNA. I took my MA degree at the school of political sciences. In 1997 I got my Ph.D. at the VJ military academy and then another Ph.D. at the faculty of political sciences in Belgrade early in 2005. In the JNA, and later the VJ, I held a number of posts. I started as platoon commander and I ended up as assistant army commander. During my work at the General Staff, I was chief of the morale department and then chief of strategic studies department and defence policies. At the time of the air-strikes against the FRY, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command put in a request on the 1st of January, 1999, for me to become head of the morale department of the General Staff of the VJ. Right now I'm a colonel in retirement. I retired last year at my own request. I now teach at the first private university, American university, in Bijeljina about 100 kilometres from Belgrade. I am the head of the security department at the faculty of law and the general manager at this university.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When were you awarded your doctorate at the VJ military academy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 18th of February, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You were - I'm just looking at it - head of the morale department during the war in 1999, right? What did your department do, briefly?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: The morale department of the Supreme Command Staff was organized based on the war organizational chart, wartime, it was meant to internally inform army members to permanently monitor and assess the morale during the air-strikes, to directly prepare in moral and psychological terms the soldiers in order to make them better able to endure the hardship they were facing. Another important task of our department was to take advantage of this difficult social situation in order to apply scientific matters and study the behaviour of persons under these difficult conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This internal informing system, exchange of information, within that framework in the army, was there such an area, such a field that dealt with or comprised certain negative phenomena, or rather, information on any crimes and violations committed by members of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: One of the tasks of internal information, not the only one, was to monitor the soldiers and members of all units and commands and to keep them informed on the situation in their unit. This is the third element of internal informing, informing about the situation in one's own unit. This also dealt with negative phenomena, any negative phenomena which may have occurred on one of the previous days in the area of responsibility of a specific unit; hence, if one of the members of a particular unit committed one of the negative phenomena or was involved in some of the negative actions that were taken or was involved in a crime, this was read out when units were reviewed in front of everybody, it was based on such individual cases that warnings were issued to others, saying that any such actions or violations would be punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us now move on to this last area that I think you mentioned, the application of scientific methods in the study of human behaviour under these difficult conditions. Is it true that you conducted several rounds of research, your institute I mean, during the war itself. Certain scientific methods were used and inquiries were made into the elements of combat morale. Can you tell us what the elements were that you studied?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is true, there was an order from the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command and we launched two investigations empirical investigations. We studied everybody in the VJ, but the focus was on the 3rd Army. The first round was between the 16th of April and the 26th of April, 1999, and 1.200 subjects were studied, the focus being on the 3rd Army and particularly the Pristina Corps. The sample was about 40 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Another study was conducted at the end of the air-strikes after the signing of the Kumanovo Agreement and the sample used was 2.600 interviewees, the focus again being on the 3rd Army, the Pristina Corps. The percentage in this case was 50.2 [as interpreted] per cent that was made up by members of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you now please look at 3D7773 [as interpreted], it's a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean by the percentage in relation to the April study you say the sample was about 40 per cent, 40 per cent of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the overall sample of all members of the army that were interviewed, 1.200 members and then the subsample belonging to the 3rd Army was 40.2 per cent, the reason being the 3rd Army was at the heart of combat operations, they were right there in the middle of the theatre of war and was suffering the severest attacks by NATO planes. It was under those conditions that we wanted to measure the mood of the people there. The chief of the -- the Chief of Staff was really interested in getting these results so that he might make informed decisions on how to use these soldiers from there on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D733, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, what is this document? It says positions and opinions of members of the Pristina Corps regarding certain indicators of combat morale?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: This is one of the preliminary reports covering results obtained by this research. This was about members of the Pristina Corps. We used these preliminary results and we applied them to the overall sample. As for the results of this research, pursuant to an order of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, I informed the Supreme Command once the research was over. We decided to deal with every sample and subsample, the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps, and then there was a special preliminary report in relation to each and every one of these so that we might deal with the most responsible officers of this corps and this army so that they might then use this to further direct their work and take decisions on the use of their own units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If you look at this table on the left-hand side we see duties, and this reflects the structure of those interviewed, the make-up of those interviewed, and on the right the social background of the interviewees?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see when looking at this table that the sample included is soldiers 37 per cent, officers 17.3 per cent, and reservists about 45.7 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, let's go to page 4 of this document now. Before that appears in e-court, I mean page 4, can you tell me this, sir: How exactly was this research conducted?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: While preparing for this research, the assistant was enlisted from the greatest experts of social psychology and social work for the faculty of phylosophy in Belgrade, it's part of the Belgrade university. I tried to put together a team around me of eminent experts in the field of social psychology so that we might together draw up an instrument, an instrument which we could then use to measure what we wanted to measure, which reflected the demands made on us by the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. A questionnaire was drawn up. This was verified before taken to the field. A test sample was used where the variables displayed very high metric characteristics, which allowed us to conclude that we could go on and use it as a valid scientific instrument to measure the positions, attitudes, and convictions of members of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, this research was conducted based on a questionnaire or questionnaires that were then answered by the interviewees, right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: The questionnaire contained 67 variables, 1 to 4 in relation to each variable, and sometimes 1 to 5, I'm talking about the indicators, about 1.000-something indicators based on which we measured the combat morale or the members of the army. We measured and checked the attitudes and positions, I mean of the members of the army, during the NATO air-strike.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us what we see on page 4 of this document, 3D733, the head -- the heading is: "Sources of fear." And in particular what we see here in the table, I want to know what kind of conclusions did you reach, what the possible sources of fear are, and then I will be asking you some questions about it in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: This is part of the instrument that we used to measure the attitudes and the convictions of people regarding the psychological efforts, sources of fear, and the determination of the emotional state of the troops. Currently in front of us on the screen we have a scale that was used to measure the sources of fear and the intensity of fear among the troops, the VJ members, during the NATO air-strikes. As you can see from this overview, fear among the members of the Pristina Corps was slightly more pronounced than fear among other army personnel that was -- this was expected because this corps had for almost a year been in the combat zone. They were exposed to greater psychological and physical strain, and they were the ones that suffered the brunt of NATO air-strikes. As you can see from item 3.4 on this scale, strong fear and very strong fear was present among about 26, 27 per cent of the members of the Pristina Corps, while for the overall sample of the VJ troops the fear was present among 13 per cent of them. The feeling of fear --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you just slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, what is the issue in the case that we should have in mind when we're looking at this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in fact, this was my next question. I was about to stop the witness, but if I were to give you my argument, then I will be asking a question for this witness. But if you allow me to ask the question you will get the answer to your question and that would, in fact, conclude this whole issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One more may do no harm at this stage. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This table here where you have item number 3, NATO bombing, we can see that in the whole -- in the entire sample NATO bombing was the source of fear for 23 per cent, and the Pristina Corps it was 39 per cent. And you actually did say that the Pristina Corps had reason that Pristina Corps personnel had reason to feel this increased rate of fear because of the air-strikes. Now, I want to ask you the following. Based on your experience as a scientist, as a soldier, and perhaps this is something that you could conclude, would there be a difference between soldiers and civilians in the intensity of fear when faced with -- let me be specific, when faced with NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. Is there no objection taken to that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do object to that, Your Honour. There's no foundation for him to express an opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the basis for this witness expressing an opinion on that matter, which is a matter of expertise for a start?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well I think it is actually beyond the scope of questions for experts. We had a number of witnesses, Prosecution witnesses, who said that they were not afraid of NATO air-strikes and that they were not afraid of bombs at all. And here we tried to present empirical research carried out by the VJ among its own personnel, people who should have had a lower tolerance, threshold, compared to ordinary civilians, and as you can see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not answering the question, with respect. What is the basis for this witness being able to make that comparison? What qualification has he got that I don't have to assess that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, he's a soldier, so I guess he was involved in the training of soldiers and he was probably preparing them for the situations that followed, and within this framework I assume that he might be in a position to explain to us what the effect of something is on a person who had undergone preparations and a person who had not been prepared at all for something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, we consider you have not established a foundation for asking the question that you've just asked, and therefore we will not allow you to seek that opinion based on what we've heard so far as to the basis for it. If the witness has been observing Albanians or has some questionnaires relating to the reactions of Albanians, it would be different. But to draw a conclusion based on his research among soldiers when he's not an expert in this field of psychology, then it would be inappropriate for him to be expressing an opinion. So please move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: While we're on this point, Colonel, did you go to Kosovo at all?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At one point at the end of the air-strikes, the results of this study showed that there were some -- there was some slipping of the combat morale among some of the units, and the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command ordered that team of high-ranking officers should go to Kosovo and Metohija to determine the level at which tasks were being carried out, to determine the state of morale, to provide assistance to the units, to eliminate those defects, in order to then be able to submit the report that could be used by the Chief of Staff of the -- and the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army so that they, in turn, could take additional measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We will come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But could we please now have page 2 of this document that is in front of us, that's 3D733.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, but very briefly, what is this table that we see in front of us and could you please explain if there is a difference between the results obtained for the Pristina Corps and for the rest of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in front of us we have a pie chart that expressed the measure of the general fatigue in the army personnel. We have the preliminary results for the subsample of the Pristina Corps personnel, and you can see from this that the personnel in this corps - and this is in correlation with what we had seen for the previous issue, fear - that they had greater -- suffered greater fatigue and psycho-physiological strain along with the other personnel. The mean for the whole sample was 3.18, and the Pristina Corps subsample, it was 2.89. This told us that this was a moderate fatigue because the mean value was close to 3, that was the mean for the whole scale that was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And finally let us look at another page, that's the next page, page 3. Could you please explain to us, what is this table all about and the values for the whole sample and for Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: What you have in front of you, Your Honours, is the scale that was used to measure the emotional state of the army personnel. It measures 11 variables, and each variable had four indicators, four degrees that were measured. As you can see from this scale, the mean value for the army personnel is 3.18, and for the Pristina Corps it's 2.89. A higher value on the scale means better emotional state, and a smaller figure designates that the emotional state was worse. This is the standard Liker-type scale and it is very precise, it measures precisely what you want it to measure. And on the basis of this we can conclude quite reliably that the emotional state of the Pristina Corps personnel was slightly worse than the emotional state of the overall sample, which is quite logical, normal, and expected. We, the researchers, expected that, but it was still within the limits of a positive emotional state. As you you can see, 2.89 is quite close to the mean value on this scale, that would be: I do not agree. I do not agree to the statements. I do not agree that my emotional state was at threat. That means that this is a positive -- an expression of a positive opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you just slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I think thta from this scale the 11th variable is relevant for the Trial Chamber, the 11th parameter. It describes the emotions of the Pristina Corps members. It -- the sentence reads: "I am obsessed with the desire for revenge." As you can see, the mean value for this parameter on the scale is higher than the mean value for the overall sample. I said a little while ago that a higher number, higher value, means a better emotional state. For -- as far as this parameter is concerned, the emotional state of the Pristina Corps personnel was positive, it was quite satisfactory, and it was a little bit higher than that for the rest of the army. There is a rational explanation for all that. The Pristina Corps personnel had already been prepared in social psychological manner to deal with the efforts, with the air-strikes, constant combat, ambush, minefields that were laid by the KLA and so on. The rest of the troops were subjected to daily air-strikes from a safe distance, and this caused greater anger among them than among members of the Pristina Corps who were under this daily combat strain. As a whole, this scale shows good emotional state of the personnel, which means that they had undergone proper social psychological preparations, that they were properly trained, properly informed to deal with all the strain that they were facing. And if you allow me to conclude, if you had troops of this kind in such an emotional state, and I am familiar with the wars of the 20th century, I had studied that for 20 years, it is difficult to expect that any crimes, particularly not organized crimes, could be committed by such personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Some other measures were taken, too, but just very briefly. To mobilise psychologists in the command, could you please tell me what was the purpose? Why were the psychologists mobilised and what were they to do?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in peacetime we had psychologists in all the units in corps brigade -- at the regiment brigade level, and that was a person who was supposed to assess the psychological state of the troops. On the orders of the Supreme Command Staff chief there was an additional psychologist and two psychologists in every brigade, one psychologist for every battalion. Their basic tasks in those units was to assist the commanders of the basic units, the officers in the commands, the unit commanders themselves, to deal with the problems that are a normal consequence of all fighters in the war, that all fighters experienced, to deal with them in a more easier manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you told us that you were in Kosovo during the war. You said that that was at the end of the war. Let us narrow this down. Was that part of the control that was organized by the General Staff in the period between the 23rd and the 26th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the control?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: The team leader was Major-General Spasoje Djurovic, he was the chief of the infantry administration. The two of us on the orders of the chief of the staff of the -- of the Supreme Command were tasked to visit the 7th Infantry Brigade, where those negative phenomena occurred, where combat morale was decreased.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What kind of minor negative phenomena are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: You see, this unit is from the Krusevac area, Zupski Aleksandrovac and Trstenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what minor phenomena you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Abandoning their combat positions because of powerful propaganda and rumours that were circulating that had been launched by propaganda centres outside our own country.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What about after this control, did you have a joint meeting of all the teams that were part of this initiative and at this meeting results were considered that had been reached by all the teams?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the established practice. After each round of control, since this entailed the entire corps, the team leaders would report to the overall team leader. The corps commander would normally, tend the army commander as well, and there were reports on the situation that was encountered. On-the-spot measures were taken to energetically deal with problems in certain units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. During this round of control were you perhaps told that because of failure to implement an order on resubordination and because of wilful action taken on the ground, a number of MUP members, and to a large extent also entire smaller groups, were committing crimes against the Siptar civilian population in Ulezbegovi [phoen] in settlements, refugee centres, that there was looting, murder, aggravated theft, and other such crimes, and that these crimes were being systematically attributed to units or individuals from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: No. Throughout my three days in the Klina area, in the area of responsibility of the 7th Infantry Brigade, there were no indicator whatsoever of that nature nor did the command staff of that particular brigade tell us anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Any Defence counsel with cross? None. Mr. Hannis. You'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, who was your immediate superior during 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: In 1999 -- I was not attached to the General Staff in 1998. In 1999 it was head of the morale and information administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Major-General -- up until the start of the air-strikes, Gradimir Zivanovic then Colonel Novkovic and during the air-strikes Major Aleksandar Bakocevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see in the VJ collegium minutes the evening briefings that oftentimes Colonel Novkovic is there to report about morale, but it seems other times you are at those meetings reporting about the same topic. Did the two of you ever attend meetings at the same time?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I would stand in for Colonel Novkovic whenever he was away.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I wanted to ask you, you told us about your Ph.D. That you received in 2002 I believe it was. What was the topic of that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: The topic was about sociology of morale, it was about empirical research, combat factors, factors of combat morale of the VJ in the defensive war against NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned that one of the tasks of internal information was to inform about the situation in one's own unit. This dealt with neglect phenomena. Can you give us some examples of what you classify as negative phenomena?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Internal information in the VJ has a much broader context than simply informing the troops about any negative phenomena. This comprised in its entirety the situation in our surroundings and further afield in the entire world, and anything that was relevant to us, to our army. This also included the situation in the overall unit in terms of morale and combat-readiness. This third issue, situation in the unit, it was inevitable that the daily informing sessions or briefings that would normally last between 10 and 15 minutes and the periodic briefing that would take place about once a fortnight included negative phenomena that occurred in certain units, sometimes wilful abandonment of combat positions, desertion from units, drunkenness on the part of individual soldiers, and minor misdemeanours, such as theft and looting in the course of combat activities. Maybe there was a disciplinary or military infraction that occurred in the area of responsibility of a certain unit. In such cases it was inevitable for the commander of the unit to talk about this in front of all the soldiers in his unit. He would use these incidents to increase motivation among his soldiers, their motivation to carry out their tasks. He would seize the opportunity to tell everybody else what sort of fate they would meet were they to commit an infraction like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as it developed in 1999 during the combat situation, wasn't the primary focus of these examples on crimes against the army, primarily desertion, going absent without leave, insubordination, drinking or drugs on duty, et cetera. In terms of numbers, that was the overwhelming majority of negative phenomena that were dealt with in this fashion, correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I talked about at least segments of our results following this empirical research, but I'll repeat now. Not a single indicator pointed to more serious crimes. Therefore, in answer to your question I can only talk about minor negative phenomena that tend to be a normal side effect of every war and the behaviour of any army in the situation of war. Of course especially towards the end of the air-strikes when people were already greatly fatigued, both emotionally and psychologically, and there were rumours that were launched by sources outside our own country, individuals and smaller combat groups leaving their positions, and this was something that was reported every day. It was based on this type of information that the morale was built up among the remaining members of the army, in a bid to motivate them to comply with their combat tasks in keeping with the combat regulations that applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, how can you say there was not a single indicator that pointed to more serious crimes? Did you review the military court records or did you consult with General Vasiljevic or General Farkas about reports of crimes being committed by VJ personnel during the NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose you have been following closely my evidence here. You see this was between the 16th of April and the 26th of April, the study that was conducted. The indicators that we used to measure the state of combat morale included 67 variables, each containing four or five indicators. There was absolutely no indication whatsoever of any problem like that. Had this not been the case, we would have looked into it, that much is certain. We looked at all the 1.200 questionnaires, and the last question was not a question actually. Everybody who was interviewed could provide information of their own accord. And we looked at all these answers, and we never found anything, we never came across anything to indicate more serious phenomena of crimes occurring in their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry I wasn't -- I guess I wasn't clear on the date of this survey. So I take it it was between the 16th and 26th of April, 1.200 questionnaires to members of the Pristina Corps, correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: No, not just members of the Pristina Corps, the VJ as a whole. The Pristina Corps's sample was 352 interviewees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I see on page 1 of Exhibit 3D733 it says there were 1200 persons for the Yugoslav Army as a whole, and among the Pristina Corps there were 335 interviewees. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So the Pristina Corps interviewees, how was the survey done, was it anonymous? Because I see there's a letter of authorisation from Colonel Ojdanic attached to the last page, authorising blank name, personal ID card number blank to conduct a study. Is that you who was authorised to conduct a study?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, I was in charge of the entire project. In the introductory part of my evidence I said that I put together a number of expert civilians for the most part who talked at the faculty of philosophy which is part of the Belgrade university. We also included in our team a number of volunteers, professors from the military academy; therefore, civilians, well-respected professor of the Belgrade university who taught psychology and andragogy at the military academy. We pulled out of the units all the professors who taught at the military academy and who taught social sciences at the academy. We enlisted the assistance of some professional psychologists working for the VJ. When I was given the task of conducting this study, I put together a total of 12 teams, each comprising five --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not answering the particular question that was asked. I think, Mr. Hannis, if he wants an answer will focus it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop there and ask you a particular question. The Pristina Corps interviewees, how were they selected, do you know? Who picked them to participate in the interviews?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: In the teams that I put together pursuant to an order from the chief of the Supreme Command, went straight to the field these team, they would pick a random sample, they would interview people in the areas of responsibility of each of these units. Therefore, these weren't deliberately selected samples. The samples were random among those units of the Pristina Corps who happened to be at their combat positions at the time. The questionnaire was entirely anonymous. It was compiled by those from the Pristina Corps who were given this questionnaire. They all carried pens and they distributed these questionnaires in the areas of combat activity. This is the most complex form of wartime research. Science had not seen anything like this before. This is not only a hallmark for our Serbian science. I would say this is a general hallmark in the history of psychology and history of psychology.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The questionnaires then were filled out by the individual soldiers on their own and returned to your personnel conducting the survey?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My investigators insofar as combat situations allowed for this would put together groups consisting of between 15 and 20 combatants, they would distribute these questionnaires to them, they would explain the motives, the purpose, and the importance for this scientific research, not just for them but for the army, society and science as a whole. They asked them to be sincere in their answers. They distributed pens to them because it was hardly to be expected that they would carry pens on them along the front line. They filled in these questionnaires and in an organized manner under the supervision of the questionnaire they would bring these back. These questionnaires were brought back to Belgrade, they were fed into computers, statistical analyses were conducted, and then the results were processed after which -- after which reports were drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you could, try to keep your answers short if my question permits. Did the questionnaire include any questions about whether the interviewee had committed any crimes against civilians?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: There was a group of questions about negative phenomena occurring across units. I don't remember how many questions this set included, but I think it was part 3 of the questionnaire and there were those questions, too, that were included. As I said a while ago, in those answers we came across nothing to indicate at that time, I'm talking about April, the commission of any crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry. Did you honestly expect that anyone who might have committed a war crime would report himself as having done so? Would that be a natural human reaction?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, an individual may not denounce himself, but his fellow soldiers, someone from a neighbouring unit might. Over 50 per cent of those mobilised in Kosovo-Metohija were reservists. It was nearly impossible that looking at the overall sample of those interviewed not a single person would step forward and disclose this information that nobody would mention any crimes. You know how many interviewees there were, 1.200. It is statistically impossible that not a single person would come forward and talk about this. These were independent questionnaires, and independent scientists from the whole world can have a go if they like and check these questionnaires. And I can state with full responsibility before this Trial Chamber that were they to apply the same methods, were they to apply the same scientific approach and use these same questionnaires, the results eventually obtained would always be identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one of those results being no reports of any crimes committed. Couldn't that be because people who commit crimes aren't likely to report it on a questionnaire presented to them in the context where they're with 15 or 20 of their colleagues?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, it wasn't our job to track down individual perpetrators. Our job was to conduct a reliable scientific study, an independent one, not just for this but in order to be able to extrapolate for the sake of science based on this war that was foisted on the FRY. Really, I must say this again, it was entirely impossible that none of the 1.200 interviewees would have pointed out that crimes had been committed during the air-strikes over those 78 days of everyday suffering. You saw that box which talks about revenge among the ranks of the Pristina Corps, and this only backs what I'm saying. There was no pronounced thirst for revenge. They were professional soldiers, properly trained for the conditions, the dangerous conditions, that they were facing. Their concern was about their families, about mass murder back home, it wasn't concern for their own safety and lives, and this is a particularly salient feature that comes across if you study this piece of research that we produced which we believed might be of consequence for science at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about that for a minute. Your chart with those 11 variables or 11 questions, I am obsessed with a desire for revenge. Why was it phrased in that way, "obsessed"?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Just one explanation, we're not talking about reprisals, we're talking about revenge. In the context of your question, what we wanted to do is to check on the emotional state scale this kind of emotion among the troops in a war. From experience from other wars in the 20th century, it is quite well-known that the hatred towards the enemy is very pronounced, and based on the experience from other wars, 40 to 50 per cent of the troops hate their opponent. We wanted to check this, not because of our internal needs, but for the sake of science whether the VJ troops, and in particular the Pristina Corps troops, felt this anger towards the enemy. And I wanted to explain, I tried to explain, why this feeling of hatred towards the NATO air-strikes was not so well pronounced. They felt rage much more than hatred because they couldn't reach them. And as for members of the KLA and the civilian population, there was a positive emotional attitude, and a scientist can draw a valid conclusion on the basis of these data that there were no such serious crimes, in particular I'm talking about grave crimes. I'm not denying that some individuals may have committed such crimes, but the sample of our interviewees that we interviewed does not support this. I'm talking about facts. This does not support such a claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you pointed out that there was a higher number, and therefore a better emotional state, among the Pristina Corps than among the rest of the army in connection with item number 11, the desire for revenge, correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Because this is the reverse --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you another one. I suggest to you that one of the reasons for that difference is the soldiers in the Pristina Corps had had the opportunity of seeing some of their fellow soldiers and MUP policemen commit crimes against civilians, Kosovo Albanian civilians in Kosovo that may have made them feel more tolerant about war in general, feeling that it is a horrible crime, it affects everyone in terrible ways, and they have less desire for revenge because they know how needless and stupid war is, compared to their compatriots in Serbia who did not see the same kind of thing. That's a variable you did not consider in your survey, correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, I talked about facts --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir -- sir --

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: -- Fact tells us that there was no indicator that any of that happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question was: Is that a variable that you considered, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Could you please repeat your question; it was rather long.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you consider the possible variable that the soldiers in the Pristina Corps would have been in a position to see crimes committed by some of their fellow soldiers and/or MUP policemen against Kosovo Albanian civilians, which the soldiers in other parts of Serbia did not see; and having seen that and the results of that kind of conduct may have instilled in them less of a desire for revenge because they realised the futility and stupidity of war. Is that a factor, a variable, that you considered in trying to distinguish the difference in those results, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO DANILOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, that is not a factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I want to object to that question because I can't see how what Mr. Hannis presented to the witness is a variable, it's not a variable, it's a conclusion. Mr. Hannis should perhaps tell us how he envisages this question, how it should be phrased in the questionnaire, because he merely offered this conclusion to the witness that he based on some facts, but that was not a variable that was supposed to be subject of a question, or perhaps I misunderstood his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've certainly given the witness the answer for your re-examination question, Mr. Visnjic. That was an improper objection to take after the question had been answered. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As far as time is concerned, can you help me because I was assuming that we would be finishing at quarter to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm checking with my case manager regarding that, Your Honour. I think I have no more questions. Let me check two tabs here. No, Your Honour, thank you. I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Danilovic, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Visnjic, you are going to deal with the situation in relation to Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. I discussed this with the Prosecution and with several of my colleagues, and if I am not mistaken nobody's objecting so that we would support this motion by the Prosecutor to have the expert witness testify at the end. Let me just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So maybe there is some objections, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is there someone else wants to address us on it? Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I just object to that because I think the witness Radinovic should be presented during the case for Ojdanic because it can have a rather dramatic effect on the case I'm trying to present to prepare for General Pavkovic. And we have a right to expect that to happen, we had no reason to expect it not to happen, and all of a sudden at the last minute to have it change on us requires to re-evaluate some things that I'm doing. I think it should just happen in the regular course of events, and there will be a break occurring between I think the end of the rest of Mr. Visnjic's witnesses and the beginning of his testimony and the Ojdanic testimony that would give Mr. Hannis plenty of time to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We haven't explored the basis on which there was some agreement about other expert evidence being led at the end of the case. That differs from the situation in relation to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Those are primarily joint expert testimonies that will be put in for all of us together. This is not a joint expert. This is a expert for the Ojdanic case only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as I recall we put Mr. Fila's expert at the end of the case already, and I don't think it's fair for the Prosecution to be put in this box because there's a disagreement between Mr. Pavkovic's lawyer and Mr. Ojdanic's at this point. I think a solution could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can't fault Mr. Ackerman in this situation, can you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but I think dealing with his problem could be handled by at the end of the case if there is something new that comes out with the expert, that he could point to you why he needs to re-open, it could be addressed at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One other possibility, Mr. Visnjic, is that you have his evidence after Mr. Ojdanic's evidence and that would allow time. It's a bit of a compromise, but it gives Mr. Hannis more time depending on the order we make, but it allows us more flexibility to make a more generous order, bearing in mind that neither the Prosecution or Mr. Ackerman can be faulted for this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all options were equal to me in this matter. The only thing I'm asking you is not to have Mr. Ojdanic put on the stand before the seven-day break, I already gave you the reasons, and I believe that we will be able to complete all the evidence we want to put in next week. We have four, maybe three witnesses for next week, so that's -- I anticipate that we will be done by that time anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I already indicated we didn't think your reason was a very good one for having him after the break, that you had had plenty of time to consult with him in the period that you were allowed. So we'll think about that, along with the issue of the timing of the expert evidence, and make a ruling on that tomorrow. Mr. Ivetic, have you thought further on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, in discussions with lead counsel we will be withdrawing the part of the submission asking for action on the part of the Trial Chamber with CLSS. We are satisfied that the Court is apprised of the difference and distinction between the two words and we will to endeavour to use the full Serbian name of the "Posebne Jedinice Policije" and "Specijalne Jedinice Policije." We hope that the evidence will show the distinction that is between those two words in Serbian is not evident in the English translation and we're sure that Your Honours will be able to follow that in the way that we present our evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What you're saying is you withdraw your request for relief?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we will allow you to do that. Unfortunately because of arrangements tomorrow for the delivery of judgements in the afternoon in this courtroom, we will have to start at 8.30, so we're now adjourned until 8.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
